description: Syntax Debuggers is a team of four passionate developers combining coding, web development, AI, and problem-solving to build innovative solutions. At NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to use NASA's open data to address real-world challenges related to Earth and space. We believe in teamwork, creativity, and turning ideas into practical, impactful technology.
summary:
Astronaut Health Monitoring System is a research prototype developed by Team Syntax Debuggers for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It provides a dashboard for reviewing physiological telemetry, ECG waveforms, heart-rate indicators, and data-quality information.

The system uses publicly available PhysioNet research data, including the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, to explore how physiological signals can be displayed and evaluated in a structured interface. Users can select records, inspect ECG signals, and review calculated indicators and rule-based flags.

The project aims to make health telemetry easier to inspect and understand during space-mission research. It is an early-stage prototype and does not currently run a validated anomaly-detection model. The data are not live astronaut telemetry, and the software is not intended for diagnosis or operational astronaut care.
details: Our project, Astronaut Health Monitoring System, is a web-based research prototype designed to explore the visualization and review of physiological signals in the context of astronaut health monitoring. The dashboard allows users to select ECG records from PhysioNet datasets and inspect their corresponding waveforms. It presents a telemetry summary, evaluates heart-rate indicators, displays rule-based flags, and provides data-quality information. The interface also includes record-level context and details about the sources and methods used to calculate indicators. The current implementation uses terrestrial physiological research data, including the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database. These datasets provide a practical starting point for exploring signal processing and health telemetry visualization, although they are not astronaut-specific datasets. The project was developed using Python and Streamlit, with PhysioNet serving as the source of physiological research data. The software is intended to support experimentation and learning around structured health-data review. Our team considered data provenance, signal quality, transparency of calculations, and the limitations of applying terrestrial ECG data to spaceflight scenarios. The prototype currently does not run a validated anomaly-detection model and should not be considered a diagnostic or operational medical system. The project represents an initial step toward a more comprehensive astronaut health-monitoring interface that could be expanded with spaceflight-specific research data, additional physiological indicators, and validated analytical methods.
